'''William Lloyd Garrison Williams''' (October 3, 1888 – January 31, 1976) was an American-Canadian [[Quakers|Quaker]] and [[mathematician]], known for the founding of the [[Canadian Mathematical Society]] and overseeing [[Elbert Frank Cox]]'s doctorate in mathematics.

== Personal life ==

Williams was born in Friendship, [[Kansas]] to Amanda Dunreath Truex and Nathan Williams.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last1=O'Connor |first1=J J |last2=Robertson |first2=E F |date=November 2006 |title=MacTutor: William Lloyd Garrison Williams |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Williams/ |website=MacTutor |publisher=School of Mathematics and Statistics, University of St Andrews, Scotland}}</ref> After the death of his mother, he was taken in by his father's first wife's family, the Tomlinsons in Indiana.

Williams married Anne Skyes, a pianist from Cincinnati, in 1917.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Ayoub |first=Christine |title=Memories of the Quaker past : stories of thirty-seven senior Quakers |date=2014 |others=Xlibris Corporation |isbn=978-1-4691-6254-6 |location=[State College, PA] |pages=5–20 |language=English |oclc=870842742}}</ref> Together, they had two daughters, Hester and mathematician [[Christine Ayoub]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=My father, Lloyd Williams |url=https://quaker.ca/archives/library/my-father-lloyd-williams/ |access-date=2022-06-23 |website=Quakers In Canada |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
After attending the Quaker Academy, Williams taught in North Dakota.<ref name=":1" /> He then studied [[Classics]] at [[Haverford College|Haverford]].<ref name=":0" /> Subsequently, he was awarded a [[Rhodes Scholarship]], where he studied mathematics at [[University of Oxford|Oxford]] from 1910 to 1913.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Donaldson |first1=James A. |last2=Fleming |first2=Richard J. |date=2000-02-01 |title=Elbert F. Cox: An Early Pioneer |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00029890.2000.12005169 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=107 |issue=2 |pages=105–128 |doi=10.1080/00029890.2000.12005169 |s2cid=833917 |issn=0002-9890|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Once obtaining an M.A. he took on a faculty position at the [[Miami University]].<ref name=":1" /> During the summers, he did Ph.D. work at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name=":3" /> He wrote his Ph.D. on ''Fundamental Systems of Formal Modular Seminvariants of the Binary Cubic'', published in 1920. He then taught briefly at [[Gettysburg College]] and [[College of William & Mary|William and Mary]], before relocating to [[Cornell University|Cornell]].<ref name=":0" />

In 1924, Williams moved again, this time to teach at [[McGill University|McGill]], to develop their graduate program. He remained there until his retirement in 1954.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Jeffery-Williams Prize |url=https://cms.math.ca/awards/jeffery-williams-prize/ |access-date=2022-06-23 |website=CMS-SMC |language=en-US}}</ref> He was awarded honorary degrees by the [[Université de Montréal|University of Montreal]], [[University of Manitoba]], [[Dalhousie University]], and [[Mount Allison University]].<ref name=":0" />

== Elbert Frank Cox ==
Williams supervised the Ph.D. of [[Elbert Frank Cox]], the first African American to get a mathematics doctorate, during his time at Cornell. When Williams took up his position at McGill, Cox followed him. Cox was awarded his degree in 1925, utilizing the Erastus Brooks Fellowship.<ref name=":0" />

Unsatisfied with the limited amount of recognition Cox received, Williams petitioned international universities to recognise his student, eventually convincing the [[Sendai University]], Japan.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Elbert Frank Cox, first Black to earn a Ph.D. in mathematics |url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/PEEPS/cox_elbertf.html |access-date=2022-06-23 |website=www.math.buffalo.edu}}</ref>

== Canadian Mathematical Congress ==
Williams founded the [[Canadian Mathematical Society]], formerly the Canadian Mathematical Congress, in 1945. Williams dreamed of a forum to bring Canadian mathematicians together, regardless of race or creed, especially after attending the Toronto Congress in 1924 where all mathematicians of the Central Powers had been excluded.<ref name=":2" />  He worked as the treasurer from its founding in 1945 to 1963.<ref name=":0" /> He was particularly successful in achieving support from insurance companies, although he was noted by many to be quite zealous and friendly and found support from many.<ref>{{Cite book |title=MATHEMATICAL CULTURES : the london meetings 2012 2014. |date=2018 |publisher=BIRKHAUSER |isbn=978-3-319-80379-1 |location=[Place of publication not identified] |oclc=1040201215}}</ref>

Currently the [[Jeffery–Williams Prize|Jeffrey-Williams Prize]] is named in his honour, and awarded to mathematicians who have made outstanding contributions to mathematical research by the Canadian Mathematical Society.<ref name=":4" />

== Religious beliefs ==
A devoted Quaker, Williams was instrumental in the Montreal Quaker community during the 1930s and beyond.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lawson |first=David |date=15 December 1977 |title=A View of Montreal Meeting |url=https://www.friendsjournal.org/wp-content/uploads/emember/downloads/1977/HC12-50632.pdf |journal=Friend's Journal |location=Philadelphia, PA |publisher=Friends Publishing Company |volume=23 |issue=21 |pages=660}}</ref> These beliefs influenced his views of racial equality and hard work. Williams pioneered Quaker causes. He was a member of the Board of the [[Canadian Friends Service Committee]] and chairman of the committee from 1959 until 1963.<ref name=":2" /> He founded the Montreal “Save the Children” Fund in 1944.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Zavitz-Bond |first=Jane |date=1997 |title=Book Review: My Father Lloyd Williams |url=https://cfha.info/journal62.pdf |journal=Canadian Quaker History Journal |publisher=Canadian Friends Historical Association |publication-place=Toronto, Ontario |issue=62 |pages=31 |issn=0319-3934|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150204185154/https://cfha.info/journal62.pdf|archive-date=February 4, 2015}}</ref> He additionally helped with the purchasing of a building for Montreal friends to use as a meeting house, although it is no longer in use.<ref name=":1" /> He is noted for being an official of the Quakers of Montreal.<ref name=":2" />
